name: Lactic acid peel

lead: A lactic acid peel is a mild alpha-hydroxy acid peel used for pigmentation such as melasma and dark under-eye skin. People choose it for a gentle route to a brighter, more even tone.

Like other AHA peels, it loosens and removes outer skin layers in a controlled way, and the skin renews. Published work is a handful of small comparative studies, mostly in Indian patients, usually comparing it with glycolic or trichloroacetic acid peels. They used it at 15% for periorbital melanosis and at 92% for epidermal melasma.

paras: A clinician applies it in short office sessions, typically repeated as a series. Little downtime is usual, and sunscreen is used afterward.
Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Stronger or deeper peels carry higher complication risk.

angle.text: People use lactic acid peels as a gentle way to brighten skin and soften dark under-eye circles and melasma. The mild AHA loosens dead skin so renewal speeds up and tone evens out. A few small comparisons have studied it.

lead: A lactic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel that uses lactic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA), to loosen and remove the outer layers of skin. People use it to even out skin tone, soften texture, and lighten pigmentation such as melasma and dark circles around the eyes, so that the skin looks brighter and more uniform.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes AHA peels as the mildest category of chemical peel, suited to fine wrinkles, dryness, uneven pigment and acne, and notes that lower-strength home versions work more slowly than clinic peels.[1] Lactic acid is a naturally occurring acid first isolated from sour milk by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1780; as a skin-care ingredient it is valued as a hygroscopic keratolytic, meaning it attracts water while loosening keratin.[2]

Published research is mostly small comparative studies in dermatology clinics, many in Indian patients, comparing lactic acid at concentrations from 15% to 92% with glycolic, trichloroacetic, mandelic, pyruvic and ferulic acid peels in periorbital melanosis and melasma.[3][4][5][6][5][6][7][8]
infobox: Lactic acid, first isolated by Scheele in 1780[2]
Periorbital melanosis, melasma, frictional melanosis (lifa disease)[3][4][6][6][8]

paras: Chemical peels apply an acid to the skin to produce a controlled injury that causes the outer layers to shed, smoothing texture and reducing fine lines and pigment irregularities.[1] They are grouped by depth. AHA peels with glycolic or lactic acid are the mildest, beta-hydroxy (salicylic acid) peels are oil-soluble and used for acne, and trichloroacetic acid, retinoic acid and phenol-croton oil peels go progressively deeper.[1] Light AHA peels usually need no anaesthetic, whereas medium-depth peels must be performed by a medical provider.[1]

Lactic acid is a chiral alpha-hydroxy acid that is miscible with water and hygroscopic.[2] Cosmetic chemists also use it to adjust the acidity of formulations, and it has keratolytic properties.[2] In peel studies, concentrations from 15% up to full strength (around 92%) have been used, typically applied in a series of clinic sessions two to three weeks apart.[3][6][5][7]

Studies have examined lactic acid peels for constitutional periorbital melanosis (dark under-eye circles), epidermal melasma, and frictional dermal melanosis known as lifa disease.[3][4][6][6][8] People also use lactic acid peels more generally for uneven tone, dullness and rough texture, which are the indications Wikipedia lists for AHA peels.[1] Clinicians sometimes prime skin with tretinoin cream before a peel series, as in one melasma trial.[6]

In a 2025 prospective comparison of 70 patients with periorbital melanosis, randomised to three sessions (weeks 0, 2 and 4) of 30% mandelic acid or 30% lactic acid, both groups improved; the lactic acid group showed a greater reduction in pigmentation, with half of patients reaching more than 30% improvement on a visual analogue scale.[9]

For melasma, a 2025 randomised trial of 40 women and men aged 18-50 compared 80% lactic acid with 50% glycolic acid over four sessions at two-week intervals, scoring the Melasma Area and Severity Index (MASI) at 10 weeks; 34 completed the study.[7] A 2014 study of 20 patients applied 82% lactic acid over 12 weeks and reported significantly lower MASI and severity scores, with burning the only adverse effect.[8] A 2025 trial of 60 patients compared 90% lactic acid with 40% pyruvic acid every two weeks for 12 weeks after tretinoin priming; MASI fell from 10.42 to 4.59 in the lactic acid group and from 9.65 to 4.53 in the pyruvic acid group.[6] An earlier 90-patient comparison of 30% glycolic acid, 92% lactic acid and 15% trichloroacetic acid peels in epidermal melasma assessed efficacy, tolerability and quality of life.[4]

A 2012 open-label trial of full-strength lactic acid (92%, pH 3.5) in 52 patients with lifa disease, treated every two weeks for up to six sessions, reported improvement in pigmentation in all patients and no significant side effects.[10]

Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Complications increase with depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, skin thinning and photosensitivity, and both clinic peels and low-strength do-it-yourself kits carry some risk of injury and scarring.[1] Concentrated lactic acid is classed as corrosive to eyes and irritating to skin under the GHS system.[2]

In the periorbital melanosis comparison of glycolic, lactic and ferulic peels, erythema and itching were most frequent with glycolic acid, then lactic acid, and least with ferulic acid, none requiring therapy to stop.[5] One of the melasma trials chose lactic acid partly because glycolic acid peels have a tendency to cause post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[7]

Lactic acid is widely sold in lower-strength exfoliating serums and in professional peel products, and is often presented as a gentler alternative to glycolic acid. The published studies are largely from tertiary dermatology centres in India and Iraq, reflecting interest in treating pigmentation in darker skin.[4][7][10]

A 90-patient study of constitutional periorbital melanosis compared 20% glycolic peel, 15% lactic peel and topical 20% vitamin C;[3] a later 90-patient study compared a 12% ferulic acid peel against the same glycolic and lactic peels over 12 weeks, finding improvement in all three groups, with physician and patient global assessments rated highest for glycolic acid, followed by ferulic and lactic.[5]

Another 90-patient study compared 30% glycolic, 92% lactic and 15% trichloroacetic acid peels in epidermal melasma, assessing efficacy, tolerability and quality-of-life improvement.[4] Other trials are summarised under Effectiveness.[6][7][8][9][10]

timeline.event: Carl Wilhelm Scheele isolates lactic acid from sour milk.[2]
Open-label trial of 92% lactic acid peel in lifa disease is published.[10]
Comparative study of 20% glycolic peel, 15% lactic peel and 20% vitamin C in periorbital melanosis is published.[3]
Randomised comparisons of lactic acid with mandelic, glycolic and pyruvic acid peels are published.[6][7][9]
